yesno.quote: Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.
yesno.note: Often shortened to "Pride comes before a fall."

yesno.quote: God helps those who help themselves.
yesno.source: Algernon Sidney, Discourses Concerning Government (1698); popularised by Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack (1736)
yesno.note: Polls find many people think this is in the Bible. It is not.

yesno.quote: The wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
yesno.note: Paul, writing to the church in Rome.

yesno.source: Old proverb, made famous by John Wesley, sermon "On Dress" (c. 1791)
yesno.note: Sounds biblical, but it's not in the Bible. John Wesley quoted it as a saying in a sermon.

yesno.source: Fable from medieval Persian Sufi poets; retold by Edward FitzGerald (1852) and Abraham Lincoln (1859)
yesno.note: Not in the Bible. It comes from a Persian fable about a king's ring, later tied to Solomon in folklore.

yesno.quote: I am escaped with the skin of my teeth.
yesno.note: Job is where the phrase "by the skin of my teeth" comes from.

yesno.quote: Love the sinner, hate the sin.
yesno.source: Saying based on St Augustine, Letter 211 (c. 424): "with love for mankind and hatred of sins"
yesno.note: Not a Bible verse. The idea goes back to St Augustine, writing around AD 424.

yesno.quote: A soft answer turneth away wrath: but grievous words stir up anger.
The Lord works in mysterious ways.
yesno.source: Popular paraphrase of William Cowper, hymn "Light Shining out of Darkness", Olney Hymns (1779)
yesno.note: Not in the Bible. It echoes Cowper's hymn line "God moves in a mysterious way."

yesno.quote: Can a man take fire in his bosom, and his clothes not be burned?
yesno.note: A warning in Proverbs that some choices always bring consequences.

yesno.quote: Spare the rod and spoil the child.
yesno.note: Not in the Bible as worded. Proverbs 13:24 says "He that spareth his rod hateth his son."

yesno.quote: Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there?
yesno.note: The prophet Jeremiah, grieving over his people.

options.quote: This above all: to thine own self be true.
options.source: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 1 Scene 3 (c. 1600)

options.quote: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.
options.source: Matthew 22:39 (KJV)

options.quote: Neither a borrower nor a lender be.
options.source: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 1 Scene 3 (c. 1600)

options.quote: Brevity is the soul of wit.
options.source: William Shakespeare, Hamlet, Act 2 Scene 2 (c. 1600)

choose.note: Jesus called this the second great commandment. All three decoys are Polonius in Hamlet.

options.quote: Be sure your sin will find you out.
options.source: Numbers 32:23 (KJV)

options.quote: Honesty is the best policy.
options.source: English proverb, first recorded in Sir Edwin Sandys, Europae Speculum (1599)

options.quote: Charity begins at home.
options.source: English proverb; modern form first printed in Sir Thomas Browne, Religio Medici (1642)

options.quote: Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy and wise.
options.source: Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack, collected in The Way to Wealth (1758)

choose.note: Moses' warning in Numbers 32:23. "Charity begins at home" is a proverb, not a verse.

options.quote: An apple a day keeps the doctor away.
options.source: Welsh proverb, recorded in Pembrokeshire (1866); modern wording from the 1880s

options.quote: God heals, and the doctor takes the fees.
options.source: Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack (1736)

options.quote: Physician, heal thyself.
options.source: Luke 4:23 (KJV)

options.quote: There's more old drunkards than old doctors.
options.source: Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack (1736)

choose.note: Jesus quotes this proverb in Luke 4:23. The other two doctor jokes are Ben Franklin's.

options.quote: There is a tide in the affairs of men, which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.
options.source: William Shakespeare, Julius Caesar, Act 4 Scene 3 (1599)

options.quote: All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players.
options.source: William Shakespeare, As You Like It, Act 2 Scene 7 (c. 1599)

options.quote: The quality of mercy is not strain'd; it droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven.
options.source: William Shakespeare, The Merchant of Venice, Act 4 Scene 1 (c. 1597)

options.quote: To every thing there is a season, and a time to every purpose under the heaven.
options.source: Ecclesiastes 3:1 (KJV)

choose.note: Ecclesiastes 3:1, just before "A time to be born, and a time to die." The rest are Shakespeare.

options.quote: Moderation in all things.
options.source: Proverb echoing the ancient Greek maxim "Nothing in excess" (Delphi); exact wording of later origin

options.quote: Whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
options.source: Galatians 6:7 (KJV)

options.quote: Fortune favours the bold.
options.source: Latin proverb, found in Terence, Phormio (151 BC)

options.quote: Every cloud has a silver lining.
options.source: Proverb based on John Milton, Comus (1634)

choose.note: Galatians 6:7 is where "you reap what you sow" comes from.

options.quote: To err is human, to forgive divine.
options.source: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism (1711)

options.quote: A little learning is a dang'rous thing.
options.source: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism (1711)

options.quote: Well done is better than well said.
options.source: Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack

options.quote: Man shall not live by bread alone.
options.source: Matthew 4:4 (KJV)

choose.note: Jesus answering the tempter in Matthew 4:4, quoting Deuteronomy 8:3.

options.quote: He that is down, needs fear no fall; he that is low, no pride.
options.source: John Bunyan, The Pilgrim's Progress, Part II, the shepherd boy's song (1684)

options.quote: Cast thy bread upon the waters: for thou shalt find it after many days.
options.source: Ecclesiastes 11:1 (KJV)

options.quote: The mind is its own place, and in itself can make a heav'n of hell, a hell of heav'n.
options.source: John Milton, Paradise Lost, Book 1 (1667)

options.quote: Man proposes, but God disposes.
options.source: Thomas à Kempis, The Imitation of Christ, Book 1 Chapter 19 (c. 1420)

choose.note: Ecclesiastes 11:1. The decoys come from John Bunyan, John Milton and Thomas à Kempis.

options.quote: The better part of valour is discretion.
options.source: William Shakespeare, Henry IV Part 1, Act 5 Scene 4 (c. 1597)

options.quote: Fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
options.source: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Criticism (1711)

options.quote: Cowards die many times before their deaths; the valiant never taste of death but once.
options.source: William Shakespeare, Julius Caesar, Act 2 Scene 2 (1599)

options.quote: The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong.
options.source: Ecclesiastes 9:11 (KJV)

choose.note: Ecclesiastes 9:11 goes on: "but time and chance happeneth to them all."

options.quote: Diligence is the mother of good luck.
options.source: Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard's Almanack (1736)

options.quote: Go to the ant, thou sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise.
options.source: Proverbs 6:6 (KJV)

options.quote: Little strokes fell great oaks.
options.source: Benjamin Franklin, The Way to Wealth (1758)

options.quote: Lost time is never found again.
options.source: Benjamin Franklin, The Way to Wealth (1758)

choose.note: Proverbs 6:6. The three decoys are all from Benjamin Franklin's Poor Richard.

options.quote: Hope springs eternal in the human breast.
options.source: Alexander Pope, An Essay on Man, Epistle 1 (1733)

options.quote: They also serve who only stand and wait.
options.source: John Milton, sonnet "When I consider how my light is spent" (published 1673)

options.quote: The course of true love never did run smooth.
options.source: William Shakespeare, A Midsummer Night's Dream, Act 1 Scene 1 (c. 1595)

options.quote: Hope deferred maketh the heart sick.
options.source: Proverbs 13:12 (KJV)

choose.note: Proverbs 13:12. Pope, Milton and Shakespeare supplied the decoys.

options.quote: With coarse rice to eat, with water to drink, and my bended arm for a pillow; I have still joy in the midst of these things.
options.source: Confucius, Analects, Book 7 (James Legge translation)

options.quote: Better is a dinner of herbs where love is, than a stalled ox and hatred therewith.
options.source: Proverbs 15:17 (KJV)

options.quote: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.
options.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 2 (Richard Gummere translation)

options.quote: Very little is needed to make a happy life.
options.source: Marcus Aurelius, Meditations, Book 7.67 (English translation)

choose.note: Proverbs 15:17: a simple meal with love beats a feast with hatred.

options.quote: No man is an island, entire of itself.
options.source: John Donne, Devotions upon Emergent Occasions, Meditation 17 (1624)

options.quote: Two heads are better than one.
options.source: English proverb, recorded in John Heywood's book of proverbs (1546)

options.quote: A threefold cord is not quickly broken.
options.source: Ecclesiastes 4:12 (KJV)

options.quote: United we stand, divided we fall.
options.source: Idea from Aesop's fables; slogan from John Dickinson, "The Liberty Song" (1768)

choose.note: Ecclesiastes 4:12. Verse 9 says "Two are better than one", but never "two heads".

options.quote: Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own conceit.
options.source: Proverbs 26:5 (KJV)

options.quote: Better a witty fool than a foolish wit.
options.source: William Shakespeare, Twelfth Night, Act 1 Scene 5 (c. 1601)

options.quote: The fool doth think he is wise, but the wise man knows himself to be a fool.
options.source: William Shakespeare, As You Like It, Act 5 Scene 1 (c. 1599)

options.quote: Experience keeps a dear school, but fools will learn in no other.
options.source: Benjamin Franklin, The Way to Wealth (1758)

choose.note: Proverbs 26:5. The verse right before it says "Answer not a fool according to his folly."

options.quote: The unexamined life is not worth living.
options.source: Socrates at his trial, as reported by Plato, Apology 38a

options.quote: Long is the way and hard, that out of Hell leads up to light.
options.source: John Milton, Paradise Lost, Book 2 (1667)

options.quote: We are such stuff as dreams are made on; and our little life is rounded with a sleep.
options.source: William Shakespeare, The Tempest, Act 4 Scene 1 (c. 1611)

options.quote: Now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face.
options.source: 1 Corinthians 13:12 (KJV)

choose.note: Paul in 1 Corinthians 13:12, part of the famous chapter on love.
